terms.meaning: A starting value used when the user has not entered one.
A fixed list of allowed names, so a typo cannot slip in.
A measure of how much a company's share price moves compared with the overall market.
The growth rate assumed for the company after the forecast ends, forever.
Money spent on long-lived assets such as buildings and machines.
How many days customers take to pay and suppliers are paid, which affects cash.
Spreading the cost of an asset over the years it is used.
Company value expressed as a multiple of its yearly sales.

used_by: Backend modules that import these defaults (not in packet)

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports
sections.what: Brings in type labels and the enum tool.
sections.why: Likely reason: needed for the industry list and typed lookups.

sections.name: Industry (part 1)
sections.title: Industry list and first profiles
sections.what: Defines the ten allowed industry names and the starting numbers for SaaS and Software.
sections.why: Likely reason: a fixed list keeps industry names consistent across the app.
sections.watch_out: The names are the exact text the frontend and database must send, so renaming one breaks lookups.

sections.name: Industry (part 2)
sections.title: Rest of Software, E-commerce and start of Manufacturing
sections.what: Finishes the Software profile, then gives the E-commerce numbers, with high product costs and inventory, and starts the Manufacturing profile.
sections.why: Likely reason: each industry has its own cost and cash pattern, so each gets its own numbers.
sections.watch_out: E-commerce earns small margins on large costs, so a small change in a cost percentage shifts profit a lot.

sections.name: Industry (part 3)
sections.title: Manufacturing, Healthcare and start of Retail
sections.what: Finishes Manufacturing with heavy capital spending and high inventory, gives Healthcare numbers with long insurance payment delays, and starts the Retail profile.
sections.why: Likely reason: these industries have distinct capital needs and payment timing.
sections.watch_out: Healthcare's 75 receivable days strongly affect cash flow, so a user switching industries will see a large change. The rest of the Retail profile was not reviewed.

sections.name: Industry (part 4)
sections.title: Industry benchmark numbers, part 4
sections.what: Finishes the default numbers for one industry (its name is above this section) and starts the Fintech block at line 213. These numbers are starting assumptions for a model: cost shares, margin targets, days to collect and pay, capital spending and valuation inputs.
sections.why: Likely reason: each industry is one plain block of numbers, so they are easy to read and change.
sections.watch_out: These are fixed estimates written into the code, so changing one changes every model that uses that industry.

sections.name: Industry (part 5)
sections.title: Industry benchmark numbers, part 5
sections.what: Finishes the Consulting block (professional services, mostly labor costs), then sets the Hardware block (electronics makers) and starts the Media block.
sections.why: Likely reason: the same layout is repeated for each industry, so every industry is set up the same way.
sections.watch_out: Percentages are written as decimals (0.30 means 30 percent), so typing 30 instead of 0.30 would make a value 100 times too large.

sections.name: Industry (part 6)
sections.title: Industry benchmark numbers, part 6
sections.what: Finishes the Media block for media, entertainment and content companies, then closes the table of all industries.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The numbers do not update on their own, so they can go out of date.

sections.name: get_industry_defaults
sections.title: Looking up one industry's numbers
sections.what: Returns a copy of the numbers for one industry, sized to the number of forecast years requested. If the industry name is not recognized, it quietly uses the software (SaaS) numbers instead.
sections.why: Likely reason: a safe lookup, so an unknown name does not crash the model.
sections.watch_out: The fallback is silent, so a typo in an industry name gives software numbers with no warning.

sections.name: get_all_industries
sections.title: Listing all supported industries
sections.what: Builds a list of every supported industry with its name, description and example companies, for use in a menu or list.
sections.why: Likely reason: the user interface can show the choices without repeating them elsewhere.
sections.watch_out: A new industry must be added to the list of names and to the number table, or it will appear with no numbers.

sections.name: calculate_capex_from_defaults
sections.title: Estimating capital spending from revenue
sections.what: Estimates capital spending for each year as a percent of that year's revenue, using the industry's percentages.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets a model estimate capital spending from revenue without the user typing every year.
sections.watch_out: The result is only as long as the shorter of the revenue list and the percentage list, so a mismatch silently drops years.

sections.name: get_ai_enhanced_defaults
sections.title: Adding research to industry numbers (not built)
sections.what: Returns the industry numbers and labels where they came from, with the industry and an optional company name. Research data is accepted but has no effect yet.
sections.why: Likely reason: a placeholder for a future step that adjusts numbers using research. The code comment says this is not built yet.
sections.watch_out: Passing research data changes nothing today, so a user may think research was applied when it was not.

summary: Holds typical starting assumptions for ten business types, such as SaaS and Retail. Only the first four of eleven sections were reviewed, so the functions that read these numbers are not explained.
purpose: Provides starting numbers so a new model does not begin from blank.
why: Likely reason: saves the user from typing every assumption and gives a sensible starting point.
how: Defines the list of industries, then a large lookup per industry with revenue base, five years of growth, cost percentages, margins, working capital days, capital spending, depreciation, beta, valuation multiples, terminal growth, debt ratio and cost of debt. Functions later in the file, not reviewed here, read these values.
inputs: No outside input at run time; the numbers are typed into the code.
outputs: Default values for a model, looked up by industry name.
risks: The numbers have no source comments, so they can look authoritative when they are estimates. Percentages are stored as decimals such as 0.20 while days are whole numbers, so mixing the two gives results off by a factor of about 100. Industry names must match the list exactly.
debug: If defaults look wrong, check the industry name matches the list exactly, such as E-commerce with a hyphen. Compare values against this file. Do not rely on them without a source.
